content: A capillary hemangioma, also referred to as an infantile hemangioma or strawberry hemangioma, is a vascular lesion that manifests as a raised, red, and lumpy area of tissue. These lesions can develop on any part of the body, but approximately 83% are localized to the head or neck region. Typically, the lesion becomes noticeable within one to four weeks after birth. It often undergoes a phase of rapid growth before stabilizing and gradually regressing over time. In many cases, capillary hemangiomas resolve spontaneously. By the age of 2, some lesions may have disappeared entirely, with approximately 60% resolving by the age of 5 and 90–95% by the age of 9. These lesions are observed to occur five times more frequently in female infants compared to males and are predominantly seen in Caucasian populations. Additionally, infants with low birth weight have an increased likelihood, approximately 26%, of developing a hemangioma. Although the appearance of a capillary hemangioma can be concerning to parents, medical professionals generally recommend a conservative approach, allowing the lesion to regress naturally. Intervention is typically reserved for cases where the hemangioma obstructs critical functions, such as vision or nasal airflow.
